title: Autoimmune Encephalitis versus Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in a patient with typical Facio-brachial dystonic seizures: A case report with Diagnostic challenges
case_prompt:
A 45-year-old previously healthy man presented with paroxysmal, stereotyped involuntary movements of the face and dystonic posturing of the right upper arm lasting 3–5 seconds, occurring 20–30 times per day. There was no tongue biting, incontinence, or impaired awareness. On examination he was alert, oriented, and exhibited no cognitive deficit, extrapyramidal signs, or cerebellar findings. Routine blood tests, including electrolytes, liver and renal function, were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was within normal limits. Brain MRI showed diffuse cortical atrophy, and 24-hour EEG monitoring revealed no epileptiform discharges. Serum antibody against LGI1 was positive. He received intravenous immunoglobulin and methylprednisolone, with complete resolution of the facio-brachial dystonic seizures within three days. He remained well on oral steroids for two months without neurologic symptoms.

In the third month, he developed a two-week history of stiffness in all four limbs, difficulty walking, reduced verbal output, and cognitive decline. On examination he was conscious but hypophonic; Mini-Mental State Examination score was 19/30, with impairment in delayed recall, naming, visuospatial function, verbal comprehension, reading, and writing. There was rigidity and generalized bradykinesia with brisk reflexes, a positive Myerson’s sign, and prominent gait and truncal ataxia. Routine laboratory studies and repeat CSF analysis were normal. Brain MRI showed marked cortical atrophy and T2-FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral thalami. Serum autoimmune and paraneoplastic panels were negative, and anti-LGI1 antibodies were no longer detected. Thyroid function tests, including anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody, were normal. FDG-PET revealed diffuse hypermetabolism in the basal ganglia, thalami, and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres. He was treated again with IVIG and methylprednisolone, and discharge planning included a course of oral steroids and consideration of rituximab infusion.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. LGI1 encephalitis — “Antibody against LGI1 was positive in serum. A diagnosis of LGI1 encephalitis was made and patient was initiated on intravenous immunoglobulin and intravenous methylprednisolone.”  
2. Autoimmune (limbic) encephalitis recurrence — “diffuse hypermetabolism in basal ganglia, thalamus and bilateral cerebellar hemisphere … The hypermetabolism suggests autoimmune process (Baumgartner et al., 2013).”  
3. Persistent LGI1 encephalitis — “Antibodies to LGI1 were not detected in serum.”  
4. Paraneoplastic encephalitis — “Serum autoimmune and paraneoplastic panel were negative.”  
5. Thyroid-related encephalopathy — “Thyroid function tests with anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody was also normal.”  
6. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease — “With such a rapidly progressive dementia and prominent EPS features the possibility of CJD was considered.”
